latest_articles.title: Mobile AI Service Robots and Everyday Politics of Space
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines the rise of a new generation of mobile service robots that use AI for navigation and communication in public and semipublic spaces. Reviewing the state of the field of service robots and robot scholarship, this paper is a literature-informed commentary on mobile AI service robots as mobile media and their implications for human workers and the public, shared environments, and regulation in everyday spaces. We examine how mobile AI service robots are increasingly appearing in restaurants, hotels, university campuses, and public streets as service workers, tools, and social actors, introducing new modalities of communication, and reshaping spatial relationships, labour practices and power dynamics. These developments raise critical questions about the effect of robots’ communicative acts of movement, interfacing and emotional expression on others, the organisation of labour, and their role in the privatisation and surveillance of space. Ultimately, we argue that as mobile AI becomes embedded in ordinary life and work settings, it necessitates a renewed focus on who benefits, who is displaced, and how these increasingly agentic actors are governed as they become normalised in shared and public spaces.

latest_articles.title: Silent yet Not Deserted: Associations Between Ringer Modes, Mobile Phone Use, and Digital Stress
latest_articles.abstract: While digital disconnection and smartphone regulation have gained scholarly attention, little is known about phone setting customizations. Currently, there is inconsistent evidence on whether modifying ringer modes reduces actual smartphone use and digital stress. Some studies suggest that a silent mode can reduce phone attentiveness, whereas others deem it ineffective or counterproductive. Drawing on self-determination theory, we explore the associations between preferred ringer mode, smartphone use (i.e., screen time and number of unlocks), and digital stress, alongside intrinsic and extrinsic motivations. We analyzed data from a quota-based survey of 386 smartphone users in Flanders (Belgium) using structural equation modeling multigroup analyses. Our study revealed few direct associations between preferred ringer mode and smartphone use or digital stress. However, our findings underscore the crucial role of motivation in choosing a ringer mode, revealing multiple significant associations among intrinsic and extrinsic motivations, phone use, and digital stress. We discuss these theoretical and empirical findings in light of self-determination theory.

latest_articles.title: Towards a Communicative Theory of Organizational Consent: Two Case Studies of Consent Contracts in Body Work
latest_articles.abstract: This essay offers four empirically grounded claims to build a communicative theory of organizational consent (CTOC): (a) communication is the substance of organizational consent, (b) revoking organizational consent requires (re)negotiation, (c) communicating (non)consent is a power-laden process, and (d) organizational texts enable and constrain consent talk. Data used to abductively build these propositions came from two case studies of body work and organizational consent (i.e. two dance-intensive musical productions at a university). Within both studies, members were expected to sign and adhere to a “consent contract” – a policy detailing (in)appropriate touch and risk management procedures. The contract was largely forgotten by members in Study 1. Within Study 2, consent talk was routinized and inscripted within members’ everyday conversations. In our theorizing, we employ the Montreal school’s metatheoretical perspective of the communicative constitution of organizations (CCO) and an (im-)properties approach to (socio-)materiality. With this foundation, we support our claim-building by contrasting case study findings in conversation with past literature on consent and body work. Theorizing organizational consent through the lens of CCO shifts the conceptualization of consent as a static legal agreement or a psychological perception to consent as a dynamic, ongoing process of social construction. The conclusion offers heuristic and practical implications for future research and reform.

latest_articles.title: Maintaining place: How journalists preserve their communities during times of dislocation
latest_articles.abstract: During the 2023 wildfires in Canada’s Northwest Territories, journalists evacuated alongside residents. Spread across Canada, they continued to report on and for a community that had been dislocated. This paper argues that, in such conditions, local journalism adopts a place maintenance function, preserving and repairing a shared sense of “home” when physical proximity is no longer possible. Building on concepts of imagined communities, place maintenance, and interpretive communities, we show Northern journalists sustain continuity through three mechanisms. First, they reaffirm a distinct Northern identity and its boundaries. Second, they coordinate and legitimate shared interpretations of the crisis within a small Northern journalistic community. Third, they enact custodial relationships with audiences through translation, coordination, and information provision when routine infrastructures falter. Across these practices, coverage is oriented toward restoring the status quo ante , clarifying journalism’s continuity work and the conditions under which place maintenance takes place during periods of rupture.
affiliations: School of Advanced Digital Technology, Southern Alberta Institute of Technology, Calgary, Canada

latest_articles.title: Care, competence, or control? The evolution of parental supervision tools on social media platforms: A cross-platform comparison
latest_articles.abstract: Interaction with social media constitutes a significant part of children’s online experiences, with the potential for both positive and negative experiences. Social media platforms provide parental “supervision tools” as a mechanism for balancing children’s autonomy with safeguards, promoting this function to parents to ensure safer digital practices for their children. This research adopts a constructivist framework to investigate the evolution and operationalisation of parental supervision across Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok. Utilising qualitative methodology, this study combines archival data from an ethnographic walkthrough conducted in 2024, simulating a child’s and parent’s account for each platform. The cross-platform comparison reveals how platforms construct parental responsibility through their discursive and interface supervision mechanisms, expressed through macro-narratives, meso-contexts, and micro-practices. In doing so, platforms shift responsibility for regulation to parents as the accountable supervisory actors, while ultimately also controlling the supervision practices of these parents through the affordances and constraints offered through supervision tools.
affiliations: School of Media, Creative Arts and Social Inquiry, Curtin University, Bentley, WA, Australia
Global Curtin, Curtin University, Bentley, WA, Australia

latest_articles.title: Discourse competition and fragmented echoes: A computational frame analysis of climate change debate on Platform X
latest_articles.abstract: Climate change communication is often framed as a contest between scientific knowledge and skepticism, but this binary overlooks fragmentation within the broader climate-concerned public. Drawing on cultural cognition theory, this study examines how competing discourse frames organize climate change debate on Twitter/X. A total of 556,470 English-language tweets posted between July 2014 and April 2024 were analyzed using Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Analysis of Topic Model Networks, supplemented with manual validation. The analysis identifies six discourse frames, dominated by Action & Responsibility, Political Process & Policy, Scientific Evidence & Impact, and Skepticism & Counter-Narrative. The findings show that skepticism consitutes a cohesive but minority discourse, while substantial fragmentation also separates scientific, activist, and policy-oriented communication. Scientific evidence remains weakly integrated into both mobilizational and institutional discourse, and grassroots activism is structurally separated from policy discussion. These patterns recast climate communication as a problem of coordination and cultural translation across “discourse islands,” rather than simply one of correcting misinformation or increasing the supply of scientific facts.
affiliations: School of Journalism and Communication, Nanjing Normal University, China
China-ASEAN School of Economics, Guangxi University, Nanning, China

latest_articles.title: Measuring the crisis: Quantification-based legitimizations of public health measures and their temporal, factual, and political–social critique during the COVID-19 pandemic in Germany
latest_articles.abstract: Quantifications played an important role during the COVID-19 pandemic, not only in providing current situational information but also in legitimizing state-imposed protective measures and restrictions. Contrary to more theoretical assumptions in the literature, however, figures or statistics were not simply accepted. This article undertakes a qualitative content analysis of user comments on Twitter (now: X) that respond to quantification-based legitimizations of state-instructed protective measures in Germany. The analysis identifies three main areas of critique: the timeliness and relevance of data, its factual accuracy, and the political implications of their use in justifying protective measures. The overlap of epistemic and normative criticism points to broader conflicts of knowledge and values, where concerns extend beyond the validity of data. The article emphasizes the importance of a reflexive approach that remains sensitive to the challenges and pitfalls of quantifications in the design of future risk and crisis communication strategies.
affiliations: Study Centre for Social Science Research, Department Risk Communication, German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR), Berlin, Germany

latest_articles.title: Public Self-Consciousness and Anticipatory Avatar Customization in Korean Metaverse Platform
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how public self-consciousness influences anticipatory avatar customization in Korean metaverse platform environments. In Study 1, 50 Korean university students created avatars under four conditions using iFland: free creation, private context, public context, and actual-self representation. Study 2 involved 100 independent raters evaluating the public suitability of freely created avatars. Results revealed that 96 percent created avatars differing from their actual appearance.
