latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Loving Rodin – Tristes Amours? A Comparative Psychobiography of Camille Rosalie Claudel and Gwendolen Mary John
latest_articles.abstract: Camille Rosalie Claudel (1864–1940) was an icon of French sculpting in the 19th and 20th century, while Gwendolen Mary John (1876–1939) was a famous Welsh artist who worked in France for most of her life. Claudel’s and John’s lives were strongly influenced by their brothers, who were both more famous during their lifetime than their artist sisters, and by their troubled love affairs with their mentor and lover, Auguste Rodin, the world-famous French sculptor. Both female artists expressed their inner life and their search for meaning and love in their artworks. Their love for Rodin sparked both creativity and self-destruction. The article explores and compares their love for Rodin in terms drawn from the work of Murray Bowen (1978), especially differentiation of self and relationship triangles. The psychobiographical approach adopted here is anchored to a hermeneutic–interpretivist research paradigm and is comparative in nature. The love of the two female artists is presented in the context of late 19th and early 20th century French life and art through the specifically described theoretical lens. Following the research findings, suggestions for further research are made.
affiliations: Department of Industrial Psychology and People Management, University of Johannesburg
School of Business, education and Law, University of Huddersfield

latest_articles.title: The emotional field of war reporting: Trauma and journalistic knowledge production among Kenyan embedded journalists in Somalia
latest_articles.abstract: Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 25 Kenyan journalists who traveled with the Kenya Defense Forces (KDF) to Somalia between 2011 and 2021, this study examines how trauma impacts war reporting within embedded journalism. I argue that trauma functions as a force that structures how news is produced on the battlefield. Building on field theory, I introduce the concept of the emotional field to explain how emotions function as a relational space that connects the military and journalistic fields. Within this field, fear, dependency on military protection, and lack of mental health support jointly shape news production from the battlefield. The findings show that journalists silence their emotions as a survival strategy in highly insecure environments, intensified by the absence of institutional mental health support from their employers. Consequently, embedded journalism privileges official and military narratives while marginalizing civilian experiences. By shaping what journalists can narrate, trauma within the emotional field influences knowledge production in ways that reinforce security-centered understandings of war and align with Kenya’s broader role as a regional military and security actor.

latest_articles.title: Hoegwi (Circling Back): A Story of Immigrant Caregiving Across the Pacific
latest_articles.abstract: This essay explores caregiving in transnational families as a vital component of immigrant life, especially in the U.S. context. To unpack the ways caregiving both shapes and is shaped by familial understandings of self, personhood, and culture, this essay 1) explores cultural conceptions of caregiving through the narratives of author’s own experience as an immigrant who left their home country about two decades ago, 2) situates those experiences within the shifting culture of caregiving in Korea, and 3) illuminates immigrant life within the context of broader political constraints, such as international policy changes. Using an autoethnographic approach, this essay sheds light on how caregiving is influenced by evolving familial conceptions of identity and cultural expectations from an immigrant perspective, navigating the complexities of a transnational family. In doing so, it also offers insight into immigrant life in the U.S. revealing how political shifts – especially those affecting borders – directly impact family caregiving for elderly members across countries.

latest_articles.title: Socialization Interactions as Sites for Identity Work: How Male Caring Professionals Negotiate Gender and Occupational Identity in Recruitment Messages
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how men in caring professions (i.e. social work and elementary education) craft socialization messages to recruit others and, simultaneously, engage in identity work by sharing messages that perpetuate or deviate from stereotypical perceptions of gender and occupational expectations in the workplace, if at all. An analysis of 30 interviews with male social work professionals and elementary school teachers revealed that participants primarily relied on occupational identity, job characteristics, and norms, rather than on gender identity, to shape their messages. Whereas many studies about socialization often identify gender as an important component, our findings illustrate how men in these professions deprioritize gender and choose to rely more on occupational characteristics when constructing messages. The analysis offers valuable theoretical insights into the anticipatory socialization process for potential caring professionals and the identity work process for employees as they attempt to recruit others.

latest_articles.title: Trust beyond algorithms: What drives Italian audiences’ perceptions of search results and news produced with AI
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines what drives audiences’ trust levels across different configurations of artificial intelligence (AI) use within the information ecosystem. We rely on a representative survey of Italian adults, performed in September 2025, to analyse trust patterns when (a) AI acts as an intermediary through automated search results and (b) when it is embedded in news organisations. Our findings show that AI-generated search results are more trusted than news, highlighting the growing role of platforms as primary information providers. Moreover, trust in news is positively associated with trust in news produced with AI, regardless of the source, challenging prevailing assumptions of ‘algorithmic aversion’ even in a traditional setting like Italy. These results suggest a shift in the foundations of media trust, with important implications for the role of journalism in an increasingly platform-driven information ecosystem.
affiliations: Università degli Studi di Milano, Milan, Italy

latest_articles.title: Corporate digital responsibility: what drives public expectations towards companies’ role in the digital society?
latest_articles.abstract: The digital transformation has introduced unique ethical challenges for corporations. In response, the concept of Corporate Digital Responsibility (CDR) has emerged as an extension of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) that foregrounds the environmental, social, and governance (ESG) responsibilities that organizations face in the digital society. This study investigates public expectations towards CDR across the ESG dimensions compared to other societal actors, and examines how individuals’ environmental and social consciousness, digital competence, and corporate trust shape these expectations. Drawing on a pre-registered survey of a representative sample of Dutch citizens (n = 2196) we develop and validate a measurement scale capturing ESG-related CDR expectations. Results show that citizens consistently attribute digital responsibility to companies across all ESG domains. Environmental and social consciousness, and digital competence significantly predict CDR expectations, positioning CDR as a socially constructed expectations system shaped by moral orientations and technological literacy. Corporate trust moderates these relationships: it amplifies value-based expectations while reducing competence-driven demands. Our findings advance CDR scholarship beyond technical, managerial, and conceptual accounts by empirically grounding CDR in citizens’ responsibility attributions and situating it within broader debates of digital governance and accountability. Our study highlights key implications of CDR communication: aligning corporate practices with public expectations is central to negotiating accountability and shaping responsible digital governance.

latest_articles.title: When Awe Backfires: The Surprising Effect of Awe on Self-Gifting in Advertising
latest_articles.abstract: A growing body of research highlights the benefits of awe—a self-transcendent emotion that shifts attention away from the self—for outcomes such as prosociality, mental and physical well-being, and life satisfaction. Drawing from this work, consumers often seek awe-evoking experiences, and advertisers increasingly embed awe-inducing elements in their messages, including in the promotion of self-gifts—products purchased for oneself as a reward, celebration, or source of comfort. Despite its popularity in marketing, the influence of awe on consumers’ desire for self-gifts remains largely unexplored. Across five studies spanning multiple ad formats, product categories, and awe induction methods, we find that awe decreases the desirability of advertised self-gifts by reducing consumers’ motivation to celebrate themselves—a central driver of self-gifting. This effect is moderated by individual differences in future temporal focus and materialism: awe diminishes self-gift desirability when both are high, but not when either is low. These findings challenge the widespread use of awe in advertising and identify boundary conditions that determine its effectiveness. Our research contributes to literature on emotion, advertising, and consumer psychology by showing that awe, despite its generally positive associations, can backfire, and provides actionable insights for marketers seeking to align emotional appeals with consumer motivations in self-gift campaigns.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Loving Through Pain and Devotion: A Psychobiographical Study of Love in the Life of Müslüm Gürses
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines the evolution of love and relational attachment in the life of Müslüm Gürses (1953–2013), a seminal figure in Turkish popular culture whose biography offers a profound lens into the intersection of personal trauma and devotion. Grounded exclusively in Object Relations Theory, the research explores how Gürses’ early experiences of fragmented primary relationships and maternal/paternal loss shaped his subsequent psychological conceptualization of love, both in his private life and his public persona as “Müslüm Baba” (Father Müslüm). Adopting a qualitative psychobiographical design, the study utilizes a comprehensive analysis of biographical materials and developmental milestones, supplemented by the thematic analysis of his core song lyrics. The findings reveal that love in Gürses’ life operated not merely as a romantic pursuit but as a “reparative” and “compensatory” mechanism driven by object-seeking. Through this psychic lens, the analysis demonstrates how Gürses functioned as a stable, containing object for his audience, transforming personal relational trauma into a collective, devotion-based love characterized by mutual emotional containment. By focusing strictly on the psychobiographical development of love amid adversity, this study illustrates how an individual’s internal object world can bridge personal trauma and universal devotion, offering distinct insights into the dynamics of love and personality within specific cultural contexts.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: The Way We Were(n’t): Insecurity Bias in Memories of Adult Attachment Relationships
latest_articles.abstract: When people think about their former romantic relationships, they often recall themselves as having been insecure in those relationships. It is possible that those former relationships were, in fact, insecure. But it is also possible that people have a bias to see former relationships in a way that is more insecure than might be warranted. To evaluate these possibilities, in Study 1 we first demonstrated that people do, in fact, consider themselves more insecure in former versus current relationships. In Study 2 we analyzed prospective data from people who eventually would experience a breakup but had not yet. We found that their relationships were more insecure than relationships that did not end, suggesting that part of the difference is due to differences in insecurity while relationships were ongoing. In Study 3, we found that retrospective reports of former relationships were higher in attachment avoidance than should be expected based on prospective data on insecurity. Taken together, these findings suggest that people likely have a bias to see their former relationships as more avoidant than is warranted.

latest_articles.title: AAPOR Presidential Address AAPOR Presidential Address 2026: Bearing Witness to This Moment
latest_articles.abstract: When I first became AAPOR’s vice president/president-elect in 2024, I thought I might focus my presidential address on something like “the business of research,” reflecting my perspective as chief business officer of a research company and considering how the association might think about its financial stability and growth. Then in 2025, a little something happened… A new administration arrived and took a chainsaw to the statistical and scientific institutions of this country. A national leader sued and threatened some of the most public faces of our industry. And the economic fallout of these and other actions shook our industry to the core. Once I got out of the fetal position, I had to grapple with new priorities for my AAPOR presidency. So today, what I want to do is bear witness to this time we are living through and provide hope for the future. There are four things I will reflect on: the moment we are in; the work we do; the community that makes that work possible; and how we respond to these times. I want to present not just my own voice, but those across our community. To do so, I have talked to members from a wide variety of fields, experiences, and circumstances. I share their views, along with my own, and I thank them for the honesty, vulnerability, and inspiration they gave me. We are living through a period of profound instability in the systems that produce and protect evidence. The federal statistical system—one of the pillars of how we understand this country—has faced extraordinary pressure. Programs have been halted. Funding has been threatened or withdrawn. Statistical leaders have been dismissed. Institutions designed to operate independently have faced increasing political pressure. Many of us have lost our jobs or found our work threatened. The American Statistical Association reported that all 13 federal statistical agencies lost staff in 2025, with some, like the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES)—at least temporarily—almost totally demolished (American Statistical Association 2025). The shuttering of USAID halted critical research projects and is projected to lead to a staggering number of avoidable deaths (Cavalcanti et al. 2025). These systems were built over decades. The people who have dedicated their lives to these objectives have created a body of knowledge that is essential to understanding the way we live and how that changes—the statisticians and survey methodologists, analysts and researchers, project managers and directors, contractors and subcontractors. There has been messaging through DOGE actions and other high-level communications that the work of these individuals is biased, wasteful, unneeded, or worse. Many of those people are members of this community. And this rhetoric and these actions are having a profound effect. One experienced federal researcher told me she was considering getting out of the field altogether. She couldn’t see a path forward for herself. We are losing some of our greatest assets and future leaders. For those that remain, we bear witness to their integrity, persistence, and quiet professionalism as they continue to produce evidence when the environment around them is uncertain and unsupportive. We see and empathize with the “survivors’ guilt” many experience. We also recognize the disruption in the lives of many who have lost their positions and now face remaking their careers. They must do so at a time when uncertainty and trepidation have affected the entire industry, making it a less-than-hospitable place for job seekers and career changers. A displaced federal worker I spoke to said she feels a sense of grief and loss. Grieving not only for her own personal losses, but for the bigger picture of what is happening to federal government data collection, to public health research, and to the scientific community. I spoke to a small business owner who saw critical work that she and her colleagues had done shelved, to possibly never see the light of day. A graduate student shared with me the challenges she has experienced—having her research funding terminated, seeing fewer placements for her fellow students at universities, and being forced to grapple with new worries about her international student status. She said, “When I was coming to the US, I didn’t think that I would have to worry that scientific research could be compromised in a country like this.” Others shared: “The last 18 months have felt like a ticking countdown clock”; “The institutional knowledge we have lost will take years to recover”; and “The foundation is shakier than I thought.” I want to acknowledge the extreme stress that has characterized our field and so many of our members in 2025 and 2026 and bear witness to the professional and personal toll this has taken. Next, I want to talk about the importance of our work. At its core, what we do is deceptively simple. We ask people about their lives—how they live, think, work, and experience the world. We do so carefully, systematically, and with the goal of understanding more than just the loudest voices. The importance of that work becomes clearer in moments like this, when increasingly, we are living in a world where the idea of shared evidence itself is contested. Where data can be dismissed because it is inconvenient. Where research can be labeled fraudulent if it challenges power. Some specific examples of this are the lawsuits against Ann Selzer (Doyle 2024); the litigation threats to the New York Times (Svirnovskiy 2026), CNN (Grynbaum and Haberman 2020), and their research partners; the demand for cancellation of programs deemed focused on DEI (Exec. Order No. 14151 2025; Hsu 2025); and the removal of nonbinary gender categories from federal research (Exec. Order No. 14168 2025), to name just a few. This runs counter to everything our field stands for. We may never measure perfectly. But through rigorous methods and transparency, we highlight the experiences, hopes, and fears of everyday Americans. In a democracy, that matters. Because governing without understanding the public is governing in the dark. What we produce is not just data. It is a record. A record of what people think, what they experience, and how society is changing. We must protect that, celebrate it, and feel pride in the importance of the work that we do. A researcher at the Census told me that she was most proud to be part of a system where, despite current narratives, the goal is to “measure truth, to the best of our ability, across time, across administrations, and across events.” Through all of this, the work continues. A statistician at a large research company spoke of his pride in what we do. He said, “Linking what people are thinking and saying to policy has never been more important.” I now want to reflect on the community, because this work does not happen in isolation. It depends on a diverse and interdependent community. The work we do is the product of government, academia, nonprofit organizations, and the private sector. Each plays a distinct role. Government statisticians establish benchmarks. Academics develop and test new ideas and train future researchers. Nonprofit and election researchers help us understand civic life. And commercial researchers innovate—finding ways to make data collection more scalable and accessible. We often approach problems differently. We use different methods. We operate under different constraints. We do not always agree (looking at you, AAPORnet). We debate probability and nonprobability sampling (boy, do we debate probability and nonprobability sampling!). We debate qualitative and quantitative approaches. We debate new tools, new data sources, and, more recently, artificial intelligence. These debates can be intense. They can feel divisive. But they exist because we are all trying to answer the same questions: How do we understand people accurately? How do we do this work responsibly? And how do we do it within real-world budgetary and time constraints? Our disagreements are a sign of a healthy scientific community—a community that makes our work possible, improves it, and, at times, helps us bear it. Multiple people I spoke to talked about the importance of having people to turn to that believe in the work that we do, to bounce ideas off of, to call when we need questions answered. A sympathetic human to talk to, not an obsequious chatbot. The government employees I spoke to remarked on how important this community has been in making it possible to keep going when they felt disparaged, and in helping make connections in the search for a new opportunity. A private-sector researcher reflected on how we share expertise to improve the work for us all, even when there could be commercial reasons for not doing so. A multicultural researcher noted that perhaps our recent struggles have brought us together. She said, “I have co-pollinated with so many others that I wouldn’t have before, because we’re working through the same struggles.” A methodologist at a start-up company noted that through all this craziness, he is seeing more acceptance and creativity in our community; more openness to the wide variety of practices and innovations. I can see frustration among our ranks as we debate how to respond to today’s challenges, how to move forward, how to value and publicize what we do. Some have called for the community to have a stronger voice. Some have expressed that doing so would put their membership at risk. Some have suggested our separating ourselves based on method. Some have felt marginalized, seeing the work that they do categorized as lesser. I urge our community to recognize that what unites us is more important than our differences. Remember that your fellow researchers are seeking to do just what you are doing—increase our understanding of a given population or issue. They may be doing it with different methods, budgets, and styles, but we are united in seeking clarity, and we are family in this enterprise. Be kind to each other. Seek to understand and empathize. Show respect for your fellow researcher, even if the work that they do seems only marginally connected in our big Venn diagram of the research industry (see figure 1). Humorous Venn diagram depicting our shared commitment to research. Now, what do we do with all of this? How will we respond to this moment—not just endure it, but build a more resilient, innovative, and inclusive future for our field? This is why AAPOR is so important. Through AAPOR we can support the work and strengthen the community that makes it possible. AAPOR facilitates the critical work of public opinion research by creating task forces, providing forums for debate and discussion, educating on best practices, and evolving standards for the industry. Our work on cell phone samples and text messaging has paved the way for the wide use of new methodological tools. Our pre-election polling task forces have changed the way we conduct and talk about election research. Our reports on opt-in and probability panels have given us frameworks for transparency and a shared language for these sample sources, to name just a few examples. Our response to these times should be to keep driving forward. We must continue what AAPOR has done for 81 years—help the industry understand itself, improve what we do, and identify new challenges and opportunities. In the past 18 months, through these challenging times, AAPOR has released major resources on pre-election polling (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025a), establishment surveys (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025b), texting for research (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025c), linking survey and nonsurvey data (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025d), and, most recently, on responsible AI integration (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2026). We have updated our code of professional ethics and practices, hosted webinars and short courses, organized new workshops, and put together two major conferences. Table 1 highlights a small selection of these achievements. Selected AAPOR resources and activities produced during 2025–2026. All of this is carried out by volunteers, supported by a small staff, who work collaboratively, from their different vantage points and experiences, to express the latest information about our field. Keeping this collaborative enterprise going is what will keep our industry vibrant and resilient through these times, and it is what AAPOR does best. AAPOR’s response is also to foster the community doing this important work. We are A Meeting Place (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2020). Every year, through our conference, we provide an opportunity to come together to share ideas and network. If lately the conference has felt like a therapy session (as in figure 2), it is needed for us to support each other during these times. Cartoon highlighting AAPOR’s annual conference as a place for mutual support around the emergence of AI. Created by author using ChatGPT. We also need to ensure that our industry is expanding and inclusive. AAPOR’s commitment to diversity has helped reshape the field and made this organization stronger and better able to respond to today’s challenges. We must continue to prioritize this. The AAPOR Affinity Groups give us more ways to connect and share our challenges. As shown in table 2, today we have 11 Affinity Groups, including ConsultPOR, formed in early 2026 in part as a reaction to the movement of practitioners out of traditional employee settings into business for themselves, and the Global Research Affinity Group, inaugurated at our May 2026 Conference. List of AAPOR Affinity Groups as of May 2026. We need to provide tangible, practical support to our community as well. Last year, when so many faced layoffs, travel restrictions, and financial hardships, we rallied as a community and raised a record amount of donations to support conference travel grants. We also provide upskilling sessions, professional development, job coaching, and networking opportunities, all led by volunteers in this room and beyond. In terms of our individual responses, the people I spoke with offered a clear message: steady on, stay curious, and do this together. One academic said, “We need to keep doing what we have always been doing—learning, innovating, and using evidence-based approaches.” A business owner urged us to “lean into the unknown.” And a student reminded me that when we multiply our efforts with others, “it’s way stronger than we can imagine.” My call to action today reflects these sentiments. Stay the course, seek help when you need it, and provide a hand up to another when you can. And don’t give up. Because what we do is important. The industry has faced challenges before: shifts in methodology, new technologies, declining response rates, new forms of data, and now a double whammy of a federal administration hostile to research and the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence. What do we do? We engage with these challenges. We communicate our values. We set standards. We adapt our practices. And we continue the work. Get involved. AAPOR needs each of you. Join a committee. Say “yes” if I ask you to run for council! Ask me, or any of us on council, how to participate. Be a deeper part of this organization that provides a voice, a space, and a framework for what we do. Get involved outside of AAPOR, too. Write local op-eds, contact your representatives, reach out to colleagues in need, and support causes that support the industry, including AAPOR. Join us in this moment, in this community, and in being the way forward. As I close, I want to return to where I began. How do we bear witness to the moment we are living through? And how do we ensure that this work and this community can thrive in the years to come? AAPOR has existed for more than eight decades. Through profound change, the purpose of this work has remained remarkably consistent: to create valid and transparent data about behaviors, attitudes, and characteristics that enable informed societal decision-making. That work is not always easy. But it remains essential. Because no society can understand itself without evidence about the people who live within it. When we do this work well—carefully, ethically, and openly—we create something larger than a dataset, report, or publication. We create a record of the public’s voice. In that sense, this field helps our society bear witness to itself. One of the people I talked to said, “We are writing history right now.” How we respond to this moment is something future researchers will examine. They will seek to understand the foundations of our systems that produce evidence. They will ask how those systems were challenged. And they will ask what we did in response. Our responsibility is to strengthen what we do, improve our tools, defend our standards, and support one another. We continue by doing what this field has always done: help the public be heard, help society understand itself, and strengthen the democracy that depends on both.
affiliations: Chief Business Officer, SSRS , Glen Mills, PA,

latest_articles.title: The influence of recommendation source on psychological reactance: a study among Black, Latino, and White participants
latest_articles.abstract: We answered scholars’ call to extend psychological reactance theory (PRT) by examining how recommendation sources – interpersonal or organizational with varying levels of expertise – impact freedom threat perceptions among a diverse sample of Black/African American, Hispanic/Latino/a, and White participants. Participants (N = 1,229) were randomly assigned to one message in a 4 source (friend, doctor, trusted health organization, and non-health organization) by 2 freedom-threatening language (aggravated and mitigated) web-based experiment across two topics (fruit/vegetables and exercise). PRT's theoretical propositions were supported and directly comparable across participants and sources. Freedom threat perceptions differed across sources and participants. Our findings underscore the importance of considering both source type and audience diversity and highlight a novel source-based strategy to reduce freedom threat and improve recommendation acceptance.

latest_articles.title: Nostalgia bait and the political economy of time: Future shock in algorithmic culture
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how platform capitalism transforms temporal distress into economic value through “nostalgia bait”—algorithmically optimized content that remediates recent cultural artefacts to extract engagement from users experiencing technological acceleration. Integrating Toffler's (1970) concept of future shock with Sharma's (2014) power-chronography, the research demonstrates how platforms incorporate the psychological conditions they claim to address, converting temporal anxiety into a core profit mechanism. Using dual methods—thematic analysis of 5610 TikTok comments and semi-structured interviews with ten music industry professionals—the study traces recursive relationships between user temporal displacement and creator labor constraints. Findings reveal three dynamics of temporal exploitation: (1) platforms commodify psychological responses to acceleration through manufactured nostalgia, with 42% of comments expressing temporal displacement; (2) algorithmic systems restructure creative labor through recommendation dependencies, compelling producers to optimize content around seven-second attention windows and content calendar logic rather than artistic vision; (3) embodied nostalgic affect becomes extractable behavioral data through the standardization of sensory language, including phrases such as “unexplainable chills” and “core memory.” The research advances three theoretical contributions: extending future shock theory to demonstrate how conditions identified in 1970 become engineered features of 21st-century business models; operationalizing power-chronography through empirical analysis of platform temporal architectures; and systematically connecting production and consumption dynamics to reveal self-reinforcing cycles of extraction. The findings carry implications for temporal sovereignty in algorithmic culture and for the development of alternative infrastructures oriented toward human continuity rather than platform profit.
affiliations: University of Nottingham Ningbo China, Ningbo, China

latest_articles.title: Online Social Anxiety in the Digital Age: Transitions, Predictors, and Mental Health Associations in Emerging Adulthood
latest_articles.abstract: Background: Online social anxiety (OSA), a multidimensional form of social evaluative anxiety in online social contexts, disproportionately affects emerging adults who constitute the largest active group of media users and face heightened psychological sensitivity due to growing pressures and immature sociocognitive regulation during the transition to adulthood. However, its heterogeneity, transitions, and longitudinal associations with mental health outcomes remain underexplored. Methods: This study utilized data from two waves of a three-wave longitudinal survey, with 849 Chinese participants ( Mean age = 21.6 years; 50.4 percent female) assessed at 4-month intervals. Individuals were classified using latent profile analysis and the stability and changes of profiles were assessed via latent transition analysis (LTA). Multinomial logistic regressions were conducted separately at baseline and follow-up to identify correlates of profile membership. Predictors of profile transitions were examined using manual three-step LTA models, and associations between latent transition patterns and follow-up mental health outcomes were examined using BCH-LTA distal outcome analyses controlling for the corresponding baseline symptom level. Results: Four profiles of OSA were identified: low, privacy-sensitive, moderate-high, and high OSA. Extreme profiles (low/high OSA) showed high stability (80.4 percent and 79.1 percent), while privacy-sensitive OSA exhibited the lowest stability (55.1 percent). Profile memberships were influenced by social-cognitive biases and digital interaction, particularly fear of negative evaluation and online interpersonal trust, whereas profile transitions were mainly associated with anxiety. Transitions toward less severe OSA profiles were generally associated with better subsequent mental health, whereas transitions toward more severe profiles corresponded to poorer outcomes, particularly for offline social anxiety. Conclusion: OSA was heterogeneous in its manifestation, severity and transitions. Personalized and early interventions targeting profile-specific vulnerabilities are critical to prevent the worsening of OSA and mitigate its psychological burden.
affiliations: Philosophy and Social Science Laboratory of Reading and Development in Children and Adolescents, South China Normal University, Ministry of Education, Guangzhou, China.
Key Laboratory of Brain, Cognition and Education Sciences, Ministry of Education, China.
School of Psychology, Center for Studies of Psychological Application, and Guangdong Key Laboratory of Mental Health and Cognitive Science, South China Normal University, Guangzhou, China.
Computational Communication Collaboratory, School of Journalism and Communication, Nanjing University, Nanjing, China.

latest_articles.title: Message Framing and Regulatory Focus: COVID-19 Vaccination Intentions for Young Children Among Vaccine-Hesitant Parents
latest_articles.abstract: Based on regulatory focus theory and framing theory, this study employed a 2 (message framing: gain vs. loss) × 2 (regulatory focus: promotion vs. prevention) between-subjects experiment to examine American parents' willingness to vaccinate their 5- to 11-year-old children against COVID-19. Our findings indicate that the direct effect of message framing was minimal. Messages were more persuasive when framing valence was matched with participants' chronic regulatory focus. Loss-framed messages when matched with a prevention focus-and gain-framed messages matched with a promotion focus-were more effective in increasing risk perception, vaccination attitude, and intention than mismatched conditions. Furthermore, processing fluency mediated the relationship between regulatory fit and persuasive outcomes. This study contributed to the existing literature on health behavioral change and offers important practical implications for health communication practitioners and policymakers. Limitations were acknowledged, and directions for future research were proposed.

latest_articles.title: Sociotechnical Scale| How Dreams Scale Up: Martial Law and the Living Dream of Democracy in South Korea
latest_articles.abstract: Dreams of social change make people come together in collective movements. Often, statements like “I have a dream” assume that dreams can be possessed by an individual and that the individual’s dream can be “scaled up” to become a collective one. This article proposes an alternative approach to theorizing how dreams scale up by treating them like affects, drawing from Sara Ahmed’s theory of affective economies. I suggest that dreams do not reside in individuals, but circulate between signs and bodies, accumulating values through this circulation. I take the case of South Korean protests against the failed martial law attempt in December 2024 to demonstrate that this approach can help us understand how dreams connect the dead and the living, transform over time while preserving their past histories, and accumulate embodied experiences to scale up. I claim that this is how dreams create a collective and continue to live on.

latest_articles.title: Sociotechnical Scale| Mediating Urban Futures: Reading Scales at Urban Planning Exhibition Centers
latest_articles.abstract: Drawing from observations at two urban planning exhibition centers in China, this article uses the concept of scale to explore how visions of urban futures are communicated to the public and mediated as a technical project to be accomplished through technological progress. It makes a case for how scale is enacted as both a narrative of scaling up to a desirable urban future and as an operational logic of urban governance that privileges quantifying ways of seeing and knowing the city.

latest_articles.title: Sociotechnical Scale| Rethinking Sociotechnical Harms of Large Foundation Models: A Critical Reflection Through Scale Hacking
latest_articles.abstract: With the rise of large general-purpose models, understanding the societal impact of AI systems becomes more difficult yet critical. Many AI harms are uniquely tied to scale, where certain sociotechnical risks only emerge or become intensified when widely adopted by users. Assessing these risks before large-scale model deployment is desirable; in practice, it is extremely challenging to study such harms without involving a large number of users. This paper introduces scale hacking—a set of methodological strategies from the human-computer interaction (HCI) literature designed to extend research insights without requiring massive sample sizes—as a lens to rethinking such harms. I reflect on how we applied these scale hacking techniques to examine the impact of foundation models in an applied setting (i.e., freelance economy), highlighting three effective approaches: (1) triangulating across multiple methods and data streams, (2) including participants with varying degrees of experience over both short and long time frames, and (3) focusing not on specific AI applications but on user practices such as disclosure of AI use.

latest_articles.title: Sociotechnical Scale| Scales for a Community: How Strava Mediates the Body and Space to Enact Place-Based Imaginaries
latest_articles.abstract: This article interrogates how the popular exercise platform Strava uses scale to reconfigure both bodies and places into units of community and commodity. Focusing on the design of Strava’s most distinctive feature, the Segment, I analyze how design decisions mobilize scale not simply as neutral measurement but as sociotechnical infrastructure privileging certain ideologies and place-based meanings. Examining the deployments of scale through Segments shows how this feature enacts a scaling imaginary: the belief that aggregating individual corporeal data produces collective meaning. Through this imaginary, Strava flattens embodied difference into standardized forms of digital placemaking, redefining community on platform-defined terms of athletic performance, health, and belonging. This article shows how platform providers use scale to commodify bodily activity and impose their meanings of place-based community onto end-users themselves.

latest_articles.title: Sociotechnical Scale| Scaling Digital Labor in Gaming Guilds: Metaverse Workers as Imaginaries of Futurity
latest_articles.abstract: Yield Guild Games (YGG), a prominent blockchain gaming guild based in the Philippines, operates on different scales of labor. It extends as an intermediary that helps players navigate cryptocurrency-based work opportunities and their associated risks. This study focuses on the emergence of new labor collectives, such as gaming guilds, in the case of YGG, by examining their operation within a multi-scalar organization of work at the micro (individual), meso (organizational), and macro (platform) levels. Understanding these distinct scales can provide broad insight into how collective organization emerges in blockchain gaming labor. Work performed within blockchain-enabled virtual environments makes use of platform-based economic mechanisms (cryptocurrencies, NFTs, token rewards) for financial sustenance, organized through collective arrangements, such as gaming guilds. It can be perceived as unstable due to the negative reputation associated with blockchain-enabled virtual environments. In this case study, we aim to acknowledge that blockchain gaming can be both a site of liberation through economic empowerment and a space of imagined better futures, while also possibly masking underlying reinforcement of colonial legacies. This research addresses the following question: How do gaming guilds organize blockchain gaming labor across multiple scales, and what does this reveal about power dynamics in emerging digital work?

latest_articles.title: Sociotechnical Scale| Scaling Down to Scale Up? When Less Moderation Claims to Protect More
latest_articles.abstract: In January 2025, Meta announced sweeping changes to its content moderation practices: replacing fact-checkers with community oversight, simplifying speech-related policies, and refocusing resources on “high-severity” violations. Drawing on Anna Tsing’s (2012) nonscalability theory, this article examines how these changes attempt to transform the inherently relational nature of content moderation processes into discrete, manageable, and ultimately scalable units. It identifies three contradictions in Meta’s scalability project: how community-based moderation and increased political content create tensions between truth and engagement; how categorizing content into “high” and “low” severity disregards interconnected harm ecosystems; and how geographic relocation and regulatory resistance introduce governance volatility that undermines consistent application of safety standards. This analysis shows how platform governance projects pursuing scale through standardization can paradoxically exacerbate the harms they claim to address, fragmenting rather than sustaining coherent safety frameworks.

latest_articles.title: Sociotechnical Scale| Scaling Identity: Venture Capital and Standpoint in Innovation Industries
latest_articles.abstract: Venture Capital (VC) is often defined by its ability to scale small, emergent companies into large companies with billion-dollar valuations, also known as “unicorns.” Unlike traditional investment types that rely on historical data, VC focuses on emerging technologies with little precedent for success. Investors must guess which technologies have the largest market potential and fastest adoption rates. Using the femtech market as a case study, this research argues that the scalar logic of VC is shaped by the gendered standpoints of the investor class. Based on fieldwork conducted in 2023, we reveal that even when a substantial potential market exists, White, cis-male investors often fail to recognize the viability of startups that address issues outside their own gendered experiences. We examine how investors need to intuitively recognize and understand a social problem to view a technology addressing it as “scalable,” and how this economic framing embeds the interests of dominant groups into the technologies that come into being.

latest_articles.title: Sociotechnical Scale| Sociotechnical Scales for Navigating the Polycrisis: Method, Transformation, Normativity, and Imagined Futures—Introduction
latest_articles.abstract: Faced with the myriad social, economic, political, and technological upheavals driving the polycrisis, scholars and activists alike search for new ways to understand and create change. One of those ways is through the lens of scale, the focus of this Forum. Here we frame the study of scale, review its varied normative dynamics, propose scalar shifts as analytical and empirical methods, demonstrate the value of interdisciplinary inquiries into scale, and categorize the Forum’s essays into examinations of sociotechnical scale as method, transformation, normativity, and imagined futures.

latest_articles.title: Sociotechnical Scale| The Couch Guy Chronicles: Scaling Visibility, Publicity, and Privacy on the Web
latest_articles.abstract: This article develops a case study of a TikTok spectacle called “Couch Guy” to examine virality as an event that scales visibility. As one of the most prominent memes of 2021, Couch Guy illustrates the sociotechnical mechanics of virality as well as conflicting viewpoints about public-private boundaries on the Internet. While some consider visibility an inevitable consequence of online disclosure, others uphold privacy as an essential component of digital spaces. By focusing on experiences of and attitudes around virality, this article elucidates tensions in cases when visibility is scaled across social media.

latest_articles.title: Sociotechnical Scale| “Cute” or “Completely Unhinged?” Making Sense of Pregnancy App Size Comparisons
latest_articles.abstract: Pregnancy apps offer size comparison features that mobilize metaphor and measurement to help conceptualize prenatal growth and development. This essay offers a theoretical account of how these scalar mechanisms mediate reproductive knowledge, drawing on a thematic analysis of Reddit threads. It argues that while app users critique these mechanisms as “nonsense,” they also rely on them to “make sense” of normative expectations surrounding pregnancy, tied to themes of scientific authority, the self, and affective experience. This study contributes to an emerging literature on the qualitative dimensions of user experiences with pregnancy apps.

latest_articles.title: Sociotechnical Scale| “Making Life Multiplanetary”: Promise and Imperative of Scaling
latest_articles.abstract: Since as early as 2001, the tagline “making life multiplanetary” has been central to Elon Musk’s narratives for his space-colonizing ventures. In this article, I show how Musk legitimizes such ventures through the discursive invocations of scale. Across his public addresses, Musk repeatedly frames a multiplanetary future at once as a promise of scale—as a future whose scale could future-proof civilizational continuity—and an imperative to scale toward a future that demands continual motions of scaling against the timeline of human extinction. Taken together, it is through scale talks that Musk rationalizes the acceleration and expansion of his outer space ventures as the continual motion en route to a promised end—all the while deflecting from what was foreclosed and left behind in the shadow of his scale-making. Ultimately, what is advanced is not a future on its way to be materially scaled toward but the spectacle of scaling as fantasy.

latest_articles.title: A Longitudinal Study of the Moderating Effects of Three Types of Mediation on Children’s YouTube Viewing Time and Content Exposure
latest_articles.abstract: This longitudinal study examined whether restrictive mediation, active mediation, and co-viewing moderated longitudinal associations in children’s (ages 4–6) YouTube viewing time and educational content exposure over one year based on parent reports (N = 289). Restrictive mediation and co-viewing significantly moderated longitudinal associations in viewing time, whereas active mediation did not. For educational content exposure, all three forms of parental mediation demonstrated significant moderating effects. Overall, the findings suggest that parental mediation plays an important role in shaping both children’s YouTube viewing behaviors and educational content exposure over time.

latest_articles.title: Investigating Service Quality and Patient Satisfaction in the Physician–Patient Encounter: The Role of Nonverbal Communication and Gender Composition
latest_articles.abstract: Given the constant pressure to improve patient experience, this study investigates how physicians' nonverbal communication (NVC) shapes patients' perceptions of service quality and patient satisfaction, while accounting for the role of gender in physician-patient interactions. To isolate the role of NVC, a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial design was employed, featuring manipulated kinesics (open vs. closed) and physician gender (male vs. female), with patient gender included as a measured factor. Data from 200 participants (50 per scenario) revealed that open kinesics significantly enhanced both service quality and patient satisfaction. Although physician gender alone had no direct impact, the interaction between physician and patient gender was significant for patient satisfaction. These findings emphasize the role of kinesic cues as a key dimension of NVC in shaping patient experience.

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Young Adult Siblings’ Management of Parental Differential Treatment: An Integrative Framework of Uncertainty and Attachment
latest_articles.abstract: Drawing upon uncertainty management and attachment theories, this study examines how young adult siblings manage parental differential treatment (PDT) through avoidance or information seeking, and how these communication strategies are shaped by situational factors of fairness appraisals and emotional responses as well as by the relational schema of parent-child attachment. Using quantitative survey data and open-ended written accounts from 405 young adults who recalled an episode of differential parental support between themselves and their target siblings, we identified four distinct communication strategies: adaptive avoidance, fearful avoidance, self-initiated information seeking, and parent-initiated information seeking. Multinomial logistic regression results suggested that fairness appraisals predicted the likelihood of different emotional responses (i.e., positive, negative, or neutral/mixed emotions). Testing both situational and relational schema predictors, results further indicated that lower levels of fairness appraisals, negative emotions, and less parental attachment were generally associated with increased odds of young adult siblings’ using fearful avoidance strategy and decreased odds of their using adaptive avoidance or parent-initiated information seeking strategies. Implications for fostering children’s effective cognitive, emotional, and behavioral responses in managing PDT are discussed.

latest_articles.title: Disaster journalism in disaster risk and crisis management: A phenomenological study
latest_articles.abstract: This research aims, from a phenomenological perspective, to examine the real-life experiences of journalists who have worked in various disaster and crisis zones in Türkiye. Data obtained from semi-structured interviews with 17 journalists, selected using purposive sampling, were analyzed with a combination of COREQ’s phenomenological analysis protocol and interpretative analysis. As a result of the analyses, five main themes emerged: (1) Field Organization, Preparedness and Information Management, (2) Multidimensional Challenges Faced by Disaster Journalists, (3) Role, Responsibility, and Ethical Dimensions, (4) Social Contribution of Journalism and its Impact on Resilience, (5) Professional Resilience and Psychological Burden. The findings reveal that disaster journalists are not only transmitters of information but also actors who facilitate inter-institutional communication, serve as life-saving bridges, and make tangible contributions to community resilience. The research also shows that these journalists face structural problems, such as insufficient institutional support, psychological burdens, and a lack of coordination. The findings were discussed in the context of disaster journalism literature and the Sendai Framework, and practical recommendations were developed for policymakers and media organizations.

latest_articles.title: From Storytelling to Truth-Telling: Narrative Integrity in Science Communication
latest_articles.abstract: Science storytelling can make evidence intelligible, memorable, and culturally resonant, yet persuasive narratives may still misrepresent how scientific knowledge is produced. This commentary argues that communicators need a standard beyond narrative trust: narrative integrity. The concept evaluates whether a story preserves science’s uncertainty, multicausality, collective labor, provisional conclusions, and capacity for revision. Drawing on research on transportation, framing, anecdotal bias, and processing fluency, we explain how narrative form can outrun evidence even when individual claims are accurate. We then propose six principles for designing stories that remain engaging while representing scientific inquiry honestly, transparently, and responsibly to diverse public audiences.
affiliations: SKEMA Business School–Université Côte d’Azur, Lille, France

latest_articles.title: Can We Responsively Code Qualitative Data with an LLM Aide? A Human-In-The-Loop Approach
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines a human-in-the-loop method for integrating large language models (LLMs) into qualitative coding while preserving its interpretive nature. Using GPT-4o and GPT-5 to code 36,000 words of interview transcripts, the authors combined deductive and inductive, nonexclusive coding. They found LLMs accelerated coding and produced mostly accurate results, but erred through keyword-driven misclassification and granularity issues. Critical human review mitigated these flaws, suggesting LLMs work best as coding aides, not replacements.

latest_articles.title: Performative belonging and embodied meaning-making in Africa–China encounters
latest_articles.abstract: Since the Mao era, political rhetoric has framed Africa–China relations through a discourse of brotherhood and solidarity, presenting belonging as ontological. I argue instead that belonging in the Africa–China space is achieved through sustained labor across political, cultural, and everyday contexts. Existing scholarship has predominantly examined belonging through spatial frameworks of community-building and place-making. Through case studies of two musicians – Hao Di, a Nigerian performer who achieved prominence in Chinese Mandarin singing competitions, and Akua China, a Chinese musician active in Ghana – I propose the concept of ‘performative belonging.’ Situating discussion on belonging within those of performativity enables us to engage with and broaden our understanding of a wider range of these multiple modes of belonging. This framework reconceptualizes belonging as produced through situated choices across political, theatrical, and everyday domains rather than as a given. It centers embodiment within Africa–China scholarship while expanding understandings of people-to-people relations in Africa–China encounters.

latest_articles.title: Breaking through barriers and shadowbans: How disabled influ-activists navigate algorithmic challenges
latest_articles.abstract: Despite disability’s centrality to digital inclusion debates, scholarship on disabled influencers remains limited, focusing primarily on representation rather than material advocacy conditions. This study examines how disabled influencers navigate platform constraints while pursuing digital advocacy, extending Van Dijk’s access framework to content creation contexts through semi-structured interviews with sixteen Italian content creators on Instagram and TikTok. Digital inclusion emerges not as linear progression but as ongoing negotiation with systematically biased technological and commercial systems. Findings reveal sophisticated adaptive strategies including “algorithmic advocacy literacy” and “experiential pedagogy” that transform lived experience into educational resources. However, these operate within structural constraints including “systematic advocacy suppression” through shadowbanning, automated content removal, and monetization restrictions. The study introduces “accessibility maintenance work,” invisible, uncompensated labour creators perform to make platforms genuinely accessible, while revealing economic stratification where resource availability directly correlates with advocacy capacity. Results challenge approaches privileging technological solutions over systematic reform, demonstrating how platform governance constrains advocacy through accumulated algorithmic bias and automated moderation lacking contextual understanding.

latest_articles.title: Playing with Fire, Losing the Drive: Bidirectional Links Between Problematic Smartphone Use and Grit Dimensions
latest_articles.abstract: This study examined bidirectional longitudinal associations between grit dimensions (consistency of interest [CI] and perseverance of effort [PE]) and problematic smartphone use (PSU) and tested cognitive flexibility as a mediating mechanism. A sample of 1,641 Chinese university students (55.2 percent female; Mage = 20.1 years) completed measures at two time points 6 months apart. A four-variable cross-lagged panel model revealed that CI and PSU negatively predicted each other over time, whereas PSU unidirectionally predicted decreased PE. Cognitive flexibility partially mediated the PSU-to-PE pathway (indirect effect = −0.004, 95 percent bootstrap CI [−0.010, −0.0001]). Competing models analysis confirmed this directionality: the forward mediation (PSU → cognitive flexibility → PE) was significant, whereas the reverse was not. These findings demonstrate that grit dimensions exhibit distinct longitudinal patterns with PSU and identify cognitive flexibility as a cognitive mechanism through which PSU specifically undermines effort persistence. Implications for dimensional approaches to grit and targeted interventions are discussed.
affiliations: School of Journalism, Fudan University, Shanghai, China.
Mental Health Education Center, Chengdu University, Chengdu, China.

latest_articles.title: Examining Preferences for Human vs. AI Sources in Online Health Information Seeking: Integrating the RISP and Source Credibility Perspectives
latest_articles.abstract: With the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots and online medical consultation, individuals seeking health information increasingly face not only the question of whether to seek information, but also which source to consult. Integrating the risk information seeking and processing (RISP) framework with the concept of source credibility, this study examines how risk-related motivations and credibility-related evaluations shape preferences for AI chatbots versus online human doctors. In an online experimental survey (N = 248), participants were randomly assigned to a higher-sensitivity topic (sexually transmitted diseases) or a lower-sensitivity topic (seasonal allergies). Regression analyses revealed an overall preference for online human doctors. Informational subjective norms emerged as the strongest predictor of source choice, increasing the likelihood of preferring online human doctors, while positive channel beliefs in AI significantly predicted preference for AI agents across conditions. Importantly, higher perceived information-gathering capacity was associated with greater preference for AI in low sensitive context. Topic sensitivity influenced source preference indirectly through subjective norms, whereas affective responses and knowledge-related factors showed limited effects. These findings suggest that RISP-related motivations explain when health information seeking becomes salient, whereas source credibility considerations help explain how individuals translate those motivations into source preferences. The study contributes to research on digital health communication by clarifying how human and AI sources are evaluated in contemporary health information environments.

latest_articles.title: Unequal Access and Differential Use of Patient Portals: Analysis of HINTS 7 Data
latest_articles.abstract: Patient portal use has been linked to increased patient engagement, improved relationships with healthcare providers, and higher patient satisfaction. The current study aimed to contribute to patient portal research by proposing the breadth of functions utilized and the breadth of healthcare entities connected as two novel ways to conceptualize and operationalize patient portal use, updating the research on the disparities in patient portal access, and examining differentiated use of patient portals beyond the dichotomy of access vs no access. We analyzed Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS) 7 data with the full-sample person weights and replicate weights. More than two-thirds of the U.S. adult population had patient portal access, but the vast majority of them accessed patient portals less than once every two months on average. Making appointments, messaging providers, looking up test results, and viewing clinical notes were used by more than half of the U.S. adult population. Primary care providers were the most widely connected entities, with other providers, insurers, clinical labs, pharmacies, and hospitals showing a low level of connection to patients via portals. In the United States, both unequal access and differentiated use exist between sociodemographic groups, highlighting the need for continued monitoring and concerted efforts to address them. At the same time, a close examination of the factors that led to the higher access rates and beneficial uses by traditionally disadvantaged groups-women and people with poorer health-could offer effective strategies to close the gaps.

latest_articles.title: “Communicating in the Air Force”: the National Society for the Study of Communication, the Journal of Communication , and U.S. military education, 1950–1962
latest_articles.abstract: This article explores the intertwined history of the National Society for the Study of Communication (NSSC), its Journal of Communication, and U.S. Air Force educational programs. Founded in 1950 (and renamed the International Communication Association in 1969), NSSC developed a close partnership with the Air Force’s Air University in its early days. The growth of the academic society and the expansion of communication courses in military education programs were then mutually reinforcing: NSSC leaders—including several Air Force officers and civilian consultants—helped define and refine military communication curricula. Air University resources supported NSSC projects, most notably the Journal of Communication. Drawing on extensive archival research and a close reading of the Journal’s content during its first decade, this article argues that these collaborations not only nurtured NSSC’s institutional development, but also shaped a specific conception of communication emphasizing vocational training, efficiency, and the transmission of command.
affiliations: École des médias, Université du Québec à Montréal, Montreal, Canada
Department of Communication, Lake Forest College, Lake Forest, USA

latest_articles.title: Family Dynamics and Youth Wellbeing: The Role of Adverse and Positive Childhood Experiences and Exposure to Prolonged Family Conflict
latest_articles.abstract: Families are complex relational systems in which multiple, often contradictory, processes unfold simultaneously. This study examines how adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), exposure to prolonged family conflict, and family-based positive childhood experiences (PCEs) relate to mental health and flourishing among late adolescents and young adults in Slovenia. Online panel-based and targeted field recruitment yielded a sample of 1,059 participants aged 16–24 years. Multiple regression and simultaneous multiple regression path analysis (PROCESS) indicated that ACEs and prolonged family conflict were negatively associated with wellbeing (i.e. self-rated mental health and flourishing). Prolonged family conflict explained additional variance in self-rated mental health beyond ACEs. Family-based PCEs were positively associated with wellbeing. This positive association was weakened when prolonged family conflict was included as a moderator. Practical implications for youth counselors, educators, and families are discussed.

latest_articles.title: Cancer in the News: An Investigation into Misinformation in Cancer Reporting via South African Online News Media
latest_articles.abstract: Cancer is the second leading cause of death worldwide. With increasing reliance on online media for health information, the proliferation of cancer-related misinformation poses a significant threat to informed health decisions. Therefore, this study investigated the presence of misinformation in cancer reporting via South African online news media.A content analysis was conducted on 431 cancer-related articles published between 2013 and 2022 across the eight most popular South African online news sites. The findings provide insight into how misinformation manifests in online cancer reporting. While most articles adhered to generally high journalistic standards, exaggerated claims about miracle cures, herbal remedies, and alternative treatments were common and often poorly substantiated. Encouragingly, many articles also actively challenged false claims, highlighting the media's potential role in promoting evidence-based health communication.This study provides one of the first empirical baselines for understanding cancer-related misinformation in South African online news media. It underscores the need to uphold high standards of journalistic integrity and accuracy in health reporting, while highlighting the crucial role of healthcare professionals, researchers, and institutions in supporting evidence-based coverage. The findings further emphasize the importance of continuous monitoring and improvement of media practices, as well as addressing systemic barriers that limit meaningful engagement between researchers and the media in efforts to counter misinformation.

latest_articles.title: Extreme Heat in the Age of Generative AI: Assessing the Accuracy, Accessibility, Equity, and Inclusion of Theory for Public Health Communication
latest_articles.abstract: Extreme heat, driven by climate change, poses significant health risks, particularly for vulnerable populations such as older adults, infants, and individuals with chronic illnesses. Generative AI may help tailor and scale climate adaptation messages, including for extreme heat, to better support those at risk. This research aims to assess the ability of ChatGPT 4o and DALL-E-3 to create accurate, tailored, theory-based public health text- and image-based messages about extreme heat in Canada. The objectives of this research include: 1) to engineer prompts to develop text- and image-based generative AI outputs about extreme heat, 2) to evaluate the outputs, and 3) to explore the ability of generative AI to tailor outputs further using theory and best practices. A variety of prompts were developed and tested to evaluate ChatGPT 4o and DALL-E 3's ability to generate health messages. 31 generated text and 17 image outputs were evaluated for accuracy, literacy, bias, and alignment with health communication models/frameworks to evaluate their effectiveness in addressing the needs of heat-vulnerable populations. While most text outputs were accurate, none met the target of a grade 8 reading level. Messages often included direct heat impacts and protective actions, but fewer framed heat within climate change. Image outputs were generally accurate but lacked diversity, and two images reinforced stigma. These findings highlight both the potential and the limitations of generative AI in health communication, emphasizing the need for careful oversight to ensure accuracy, accessibility, and inclusivity.

latest_articles.title: Power and Mobilized Grievance: Theorizing Revanchist Activism in Public Relations
latest_articles.abstract: Public relations (PR) researchers have often studied activism as a tool for historically oppressed groups and social justice efforts, which often earn left-wing labels. Although these investigations are vital for sociocultural PR theory and addressing historic injustice, scholarship has not yet wrestled with activism for socially advantaged groups, which has tended to align with right-wing interests. Therefore, this theoretical article presents a specific activist approach that often complements the political right, revanchist activism, as a phenomenon where historically dominant groups seek to reclaim sociocultural power through collective grievance. We offer revanchist tenets of traditional power structures, societal entropy, and retribution to explain how these manifest in the New Right social movement and its 1970s initiative, Stop Taking Our Privileges Equal Rights Amendment (STOP ERA). Using STOP ERA and its leader, Phyllis Schlafly, as a backdrop, we offer propositions of revanchist activism as reclaiming morality, reclaiming information, and reclaiming status. Consequently, this article contributes to sociocultural PR theory and practice about activism by layering ideology and approach for political nuance, distinguishing grievance from historical marginalization, and outlining a past, yet contemporarily and practically relevant, activist context.
